newsitem.title: UK: Demand grows for minor metals, cobalt battle rages.
newsitem.headline: Demand grows for minor metals, cobalt battle rages.

text.p: Consumer buying and covering emerged this week in the minor industrial metals, though the pace of the offtake was not enough to significantly move prices.
"Demand has picked up and is likely to continue so in the last quarter of the year," one trader said.

Cobalt held steady levels, molybdendum remained under pressure, while vanadium adopted a firmer stance. Combatants locked horns in the cobalt market as they again failed to agree on price levels. Several traders said the market was trending higher and was set to notch up fairly substantial gains by the end of 1996. Others argued that physical demand remained slow and was showing few signs of improving. "There are hot and cold influences in the market at the moment," one trader commented. Reported trades ranged from around $21.00 down to $19.85 a tonne basis Russian material. Support was found from demand from the aerospace and battery industries and Chinese buying.

The unrest in Zaire and the fast approaching elections in Zambia was also underpinning the market, according to some traders. But others were quick to point out the bloodshed and human suffering in Zaire was far removed from the cobalt and copper mining belts.
"The unrest in Zaire has had little impact on the market so far, with the fighting still far removed from the southern Shaba cobalt region," Macquarie Equities Ltd said in a report.

"Bulls continue to argue that the problems could spread and suggest that the forthcoming elections in Zambia may also cause problems. Nevertheless the market remains relatively unconcerned and prices are still under pressure," Macquarie added. But the bulls of the market were undeterred, believing that the market was poised for a quick snap higher, against the backdrop of tight supplies.
They said that the market will remain tight over the coming years, and reckoned the new production due to come on stream by the year 2,000 would be swiftly soaked up by demand.
"Nearby material remains tight...there is huge potential for a significant rally," one trader said. The trader was eyeing levels of towards $25 a kilo for Russian material by the end of the year.
Away from the well watched cobalt arena the other metals in the sector showed little movement.

Antimony after recent Chinese offers looked to have found a base at between $1,900 and $1,950 a tonne. But traders were unsure of the markets next direction. "If it holds $1,900 there is litle reason why the market should not bounce higher," one trader said.
"Its in the lap of the Chinese," he added.
Molybdenum eased but growing tightness in the oxide market may prove to be a lifeline to a market mauled and bruised by speculative liquidation.
"Its against the ropes but has not hit the canvas yet," one trader said. Low stocks and an expected recovery in steel production aided a slight recovery in vanadium prices.
Tungsten showed an upside improvement, though traders noted stocks remained at reasonably high levels in Europe.
Activity in the PGM's remained stolid and was likely to remain so over the coming weeks.
Indium gyrated narrowly amid the lack of producer and consumer direction.
